## Hindsight experiment — A + B + C features (NOT deployable)

Random Forest with lifetime totals added: test accuracy 0.899, macro-F1 0.897. Retrospective features are unknown to a real scheduler.

## Offline policy-value experiment (CPU-only projection; not adaptive scheduling)

Candidates ['FCFS', 'RR2', 'RR4', 'RR8', 'RR16']; fixed baseline **RR2**; class map {'cpu_bound': 'FCFS', 'mixed': 'RR2', 'io_bound': 'RR4'} (learned on train+validation); predictions from logistic_regression.
Mean regret on test workloads (1.000 = per-workload best candidate):

| rule | mean regret | Δ vs fixed | paired bootstrap 95% CI of Δ | workloads where choice ≠ fixed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| fixed baseline (RR2) | 1.0569 | — | — | — |
| predicted-class map, k=1 | 1.0434 | -0.0135 | [-0.0284, +0.0016] | 68% |
| predicted-class map, k=2 | 1.0476 | -0.0093 | [-0.0257, +0.0065] | 66% |
| predicted-class map, k=3 | 1.0511 | -0.0058 | [-0.0223, +0.0116] | 69% |
| true-class map | 1.0493 | -0.0076 | [-0.0237, +0.0085] | 67% |
| per-workload oracle | 1.0000 | — | — | — |

Δ < 0 means lower regret than the fixed baseline. A CI that includes 0 means no reliable difference.

These numbers come from an open-loop CPU-only projection of the traces. They indicate whether the class signal is worth testing in Phase 3; they do not show that ML improves real scheduling.
